title: The present English doesn't use
topic: depuis + present; être en train de; venir de + infinitive
why: French has no -ing form and often uses the present where English uses another tense. This lesson shows how to stress an action in progress with être en train de, how to say how long something has been going on with depuis and ça fait… que, and how to say what has just happened with venir de.

No -ing: être en train de

French has no -ing tense. Je mange means “I eat”, “I'm eating” and “I do eat”, all at once. Most of the time, the simple present is all you need: — Tu fais quoi ? — Je regarde un film. (— What are you doing? — I'm watching a movie.)

When you want to stress that an action is happening right now, that you're in the middle of it, use être en train de + infinitive. Only être changes:

être en train de + infinitiveEnglish
jesuis en train de travaillerI'm (busy) working
tues en train de travailleryou're working
il / elle / onest en train de travaillerhe / she is, we're working
noussommes en train de travaillerwe're working
vousêtes en train de travailleryou're working
ils / ellessont en train de travaillerthey're working
Je ne peux pas parler : je suis en train de cuisiner.I can't talk: I'm in the middle of cooking.
Les enfants sont en train de dormir.The children are sleeping (right now).

De becomes d' before a vowel: Elle est en train d'écrire un message. The negation goes around être: Je ne suis pas en train de dormir !

Don't translate every English -ing with en train de. “I'm living in Paris” or “I'm learning French” are just J'habite à Paris, J'apprends le français. Keep en train de for something happening at this very moment.

", "

Depuis + present: still going on

Here is one of the biggest differences with English. To say how long something has been going on, English uses the present perfect: “I have lived here for three years”. French uses the present, because the action is still true now:

J'habite ici depuis trois ans.I've lived here for three years.
Il travaille à Lille depuis 2020.He's been working in Lille since 2020.
Je t'attends depuis une heure !I've been waiting for you for an hour!

Depuis translates both “for” (a duration: depuis trois ans, depuis deux heures) and “since” (a starting point: depuis lundi, depuis septembre, depuis 2020). Translating word for word with j'ai habité is a classic mistake: that tense, which you'll learn soon, would mean it's over.

Asking the question

QuestionAsks forAnswer
Depuis quand tu habites ici ?a starting point (since when?)Depuis janvier.
Depuis combien de temps tu habites ici ?a duration (how long?)Depuis six mois.

Ça fait… que

In speech, you'll often hear the same idea with ça fait + duration + que + present, with the duration at the front: Ça fait trois ans que j'habite ici (It's been three years that I've lived here). Que becomes qu' before a vowel: Ça fait deux mois qu'il apprend le français.

Ask yourself: is it still going on? If yes, French uses the present with depuis, even if English uses “have been”.

", "

Venir de + infinitive: just

To say that something has just happened, French uses venir de + infinitive. It's the mirror image of aller + infinitive: you're “coming from” the action.

venir de + infinitiveEnglish
jeviens d'arriverI've just arrived
tuviens de mangeryou've just eaten
il / elle / onvient de partirhe / she has, we've just left
nousvenons de finirwe've just finished
vousvenez de rentreryou've just got home
ils / ellesviennent de téléphonerthey've just phoned

Pronouns go before the infinitive, as usual: Je viens de me lever (I've just got up), Le message ? Je viens de le lire. Careful: venir de + a place means to come from: Je viens de Lyon (I'm from Lyon). Only an infinitive after de gives the meaning “just”.

Just did, doing now, going to do

You now have three ways to place an action around the present moment:

Just beforeRight nowJust after
Je viens de manger.Je suis en train de faire la vaisselle.Je vais me coucher.
I've just eaten.I'm doing the dishes.I'm going to go to bed.
— Allô ? Tu es où ? — Je viens d'arriver à la gare. Je suis en train de chercher un taxi.— Hello? Where are you? — I've just arrived at the station. I'm looking for a taxi.

On the phone, Je viens de… is everywhere: Il vient de sortir (He's just gone out), Elle vient de partir. It's a great way to talk about the recent past before you learn the past tenses.
